idiom_name: Iterator::filter (lazy Filter adapter) over FnMut(&Item) -> bool closures; Vec::retain for in-place
implementation_notes: The criterion is any closure implementing FnMut(&Self::Item) -> bool, and Iterator::filter returns a lazy Filter<Self, P> adapter that stores the predicate and does nothing until it is consumed - so a filter is literally a first-class value that composes with map/take without intermediate allocations. Vec::retain (and retain_mut) applies the same criterion in place while compacting the buffer, and filter_map handles criteria that also transform (returning Option). A container-typed filtered copy is a method collecting the filtered iterator into Self, preserving identity. Because Filter is generic over the closure type, storing heterogeneous criteria requires boxing (Box<dyn Fn(&T) -> bool> or impl Fn in return position), which is where the pattern's object form reappears; borrow rules mean a predicate that needs data it does not own must capture it or take &T.
pitfalls: Iterators are lazy and #[must_use]: a filtered iterator that is never consumed performs no work, and a predicate's side effects (or panics) happen at the consumption point, not at the call site.

The predicate receives &Item, so filtering cannot mutate or move elements; criteria that must transform use filter_map, and criteria that must see the value by value need a clone or an owned iteration.

Storing mixed criteria erases the type: Box<dyn Fn(&Threat) -> bool> costs an indirect call and forces a lifetime/'static bound on captures, so prefer generics (or an enum of named criteria) unless the set really is open.

collect() from an iterator of references yields references - a container of the same type needs cloned()/to_owned(), and forgetting it turns a cheap filter into a borrow-checker fight; Vec::retain instead mutates in place and drops rejected elements, so their Drop side effects run.
